title: The Lesson I Learned From The Great Commission
paragraphs: The Lesson I Learned From The Great Commission
Before Jesus ascended to heaven, He gathered His disciples for one final moment.

Not in a palace.
Not in a temple.
But on a mountain.

These were ordinary men.
Former fishermen.
A tax collector.
Men who had doubted, failed, argued, and even run away when things got hard.
And yet these were the very people Jesus chose for His final words.
That alone is already a lesson.

Because the mission of God has never been built on perfect people.
It has always been built on surrendered people.
Matthew 28:18–20 records one of the most important moments in the entire Bible.
Jesus said:

“All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me.
Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you.
And surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age.”
But here is the lesson that struck me the most.
The gospel was never meant to stop with us.
Many people think the Christian life ends the moment they receive salvation.

They think faith is only about being forgiven.
About going to church.
About reading the Bible.
About praying.
And yes, those things matter deeply.
But Jesus did not give His final command to create spectators.
He gave it to create disciple-makers.
The moment Jesus said “Go,” He made something clear:
Faith that stays still eventually becomes faith that grows cold.

Because the message of Jesus was never designed to be hidden.
It was designed to move.

From heart to heart.
From city to city.
From generation to generation.
Think about it.
If the disciples had kept the message to themselves, Christianity would have ended on that mountain.

No churches.
No missionaries.
No Bibles translated into languages around the world.
No believers in cities and villages across the earth.
The gospel reached us because someone obeyed the Great Commission before us.
Someone preached.
Someone shared.
Someone discipled.
Someone refused to keep quiet about what Jesus had done.
And now the same responsibility rests on us.
But there is something else powerful in what Jesus said.
Before He gave the command, He made a declaration:
“All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me.”
In other words, the mission does not start with our ability.
It starts with His authority.
That means we do not share the gospel because we feel confident.
We share the gospel because Jesus is Lord.
And that changes everything.
Some people hesitate to talk about their faith because they feel unqualified.
They think:

“I don’t know enough Bible.”
“I’m not a preacher.”
“I’m not a missionary.”
“I’m not good at speaking.”
But look again at who Jesus sent.
These were not religious elites.
They were ordinary people who had simply walked with Him.
That means the Great Commission was never meant for a small group of professionals.
It was meant for every follower of Christ.

Parents discipling children.
Friends sharing with friends.
Believers encouraging coworkers.
Christians living lives that point people to Jesus.
The mission of God spreads through everyday faithfulness.
And here is another part of the command that many people overlook.
Jesus did not say:
“Go and collect converts.”
He said:
“Go and make disciples.”
That is deeper.
A disciple is not just someone who hears about Jesus.
A disciple is someone who learns to follow Him.
Which means the Great Commission is not about chasing numbers.
It is about building lives.
Teaching people how to obey Christ.
Helping people grow in faith.
Walking with people as they mature spiritually.
In a world obsessed with quick results, Jesus commanded something slower but far stronger.
Transformation.
And then comes the promise that makes this mission possible.
Jesus said:
“And surely I am with you always.”
Think about that.

The same Jesus who calmed storms.
Healed the sick.
Raised the dead.
Conquered the grave.
That same Jesus promises to be present with those who carry His mission.
We are not sent alone.
We are sent with His presence.
Which means every act of sharing the gospel is more than a conversation.
It is participation in the work of God Himself.
So the lesson I learned from the Great Commission is this:
A faith that never goes will eventually stop growing.
The gospel is not just a gift to receive.
It is a mission to carry.
If Jesus has changed your life, someone else should hear about it.
If Jesus has forgiven your past, someone else should know that forgiveness is possible.
If Jesus has given you hope, someone else should hear that hope still exists.
Because somewhere right now…
Someone is searching for truth.
Someone is drowning in guilt.
Someone is wondering if God still cares.
Someone is waiting for the message that changed your life.
And that message was never meant to stay with you.
The Great Commission is not just a command from Jesus.
It is an invitation.
An invitation to take part in the greatest mission in history.
The mission of bringing the good news of salvation to the world.
And it continues today through ordinary believers who choose obedience over silence.
So the real question is this:
Will we keep the gospel comfortable…
Or will we carry it courageously?

“Go therefore and make disciples of all nations.”
— Matthew 28:19
Engagement Question
If Jesus commanded us to make disciples, what is one simple way you can share your faith with someone this week?
